status: source preparation only; no records admitted or repository files modified
scope: Three selectively researched candidates from the wave 11 capability queue, compared against live discovery text and open leads. Neither the three cases nor the comparison inventory is exhaustive.

cases.proposed_scope: A named Māori pātaka at Te Hape, Lake Rotoiti, attributed to a named Ngāti Makino carver and of significance to Ngāti Pikiao, as a historically bounded witness to a community storage and cultural building tradition.
cases.date_and_witness: Te Papa’s catalogue assigns carving to 1845–1855 and says about 1850. This dates the named object, not the origin of Māori storehouses, the introduction of a food plant, or the start of food storage. The pātaka was later moved and restored in 1934.

sources_inspected.title: Te Tākinga pātaka
sources_inspected.publisher: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa
sources_inspected.supports: Named building, approximate 1845–1855 carving by Te Hārete Te Whanarere, Ngāti Makino association, location at Te Hape, status for Ngāti Pikiao, subsequent 1886 acquisition and 1934 restoration.

sources_inspected.title: Matariki teaching resource: Storing kai
sources_inspected.publisher: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa
sources_inspected.supports: General account of food storage in pātaka and raised storage protecting food from pests and weather; it does not establish the contents of Te Tākinga specifically.

sources_inspected.title: Pātaka, 1840s
sources_inspected.publisher: Te Ara Encyclopedia of New Zealand
sources_inspected.supports: Contemporary sketches depict several different regional storehouses; their exact contents are stated as likely or probable rather than proven.

cases.actor_and_access_questions: Carver is Te Hārete Te Whanarere, not automatically the sole builder, owner, designer or food user. Museum describes transfer and later acquisition; do not treat present-day dimensions or restoration as exact original measurements without corroboration. Investigate named community perspectives and evidence of this pātaka’s original contents, siting and use. Do not infer unrestricted communal access or use for kūmara in this individual building.

nearest_records.relationship: Earlier Jordanian raised storage; shared general capability, not evidence of transmission or common origin.

cases.admission_assessment: Distinct documented Māori community architectural and cultural case; strongest admission claim is the named storehouse, with generic food-storage function clearly separated from its unverified contents. If the project requires direct evidence of food storage in the named object, seek further community-sourced material first.

cases.proposed_scope: Engaruka landscape in northern Tanzania: integrated channels, phased dry-stone check dams, floodwater and sediment capture, with some fields subject to different irrigation regimes.
cases.date_and_witness: Lang and Stump’s 2017 paper characterizes the investigated historical landscape as 15th–18th centuries, occupied for approximately 400 years before eighteenth-century abandonment. These are contextual chronology and interpretations for a large landscape; they do not directly date each studied wall or identify the beginning of regional irrigation.

sources_inspected.title: Geoarchaeological evidence for the construction, irrigation, cultivation, and resilience of 15th–18th century AD terraced landscape at Engaruka, Tanzania
sources_inspected.locator: Introduction; results and discussion, sections 4 and 11; conclusions
sources_inspected.supports: Excavation and soil analysis support phased sediment retention behind check dams and variable irrigation. The article reports more than 1,000 ha of sediment traps as a landscape-level estimate, not a directly dated area attributable to one period or farm.

cases.actor_and_access_questions: The paper attributes construction and cultivation to inhabitants but does not identify a named builder, funder, ethnic identity or formal water rights system. Seek direct dated deposits and locally authored knowledge before allocating specific periods to particular walls. Abandonment causes and adaptation to wet versus dry conditions remain hypotheses, not proof of ecological collapse or sustainability.

nearest_records.relationship: A separate Mexican raised wetland field system; no demonstrated transmission.
Water-user cooperation and Balinese irrigation; no basis to import its institutions to Engaruka.
Earlier water storage, not the same sediment-capture terrace complex.

cases.admission_assessment: Strong distinct regional capability candidate with archaeologically inferred construction sequence; chronology should remain a broad contextual range unless original dated features can be tied more narrowly to the chosen claim.

cases.proposed_scope: A Snaketown-area Hohokam network that diverted and distributed water through main, branch and lateral canals along the Middle Gila River.
cases.date_and_witness: Zhu, Woodson and Ertsen adopt Woodson’s archaeological chronology and reconstruct an Early Pioneer canal in 450–650 CE and expansion by 750–850 CE. These are period-level interpretations, not direct radiocarbon dates for every channel or a first invention of irrigation in the Americas.

sources_inspected.title: Reconstructing Ancient Hohokam Irrigation Systems in the Middle Gila River Valley, Arizona, United States of America
sources_inspected.locator: Case selection and chronology; methods; conclusions and acknowledgment
sources_inspected.supports: The study uses mapped canal systems and archaeology to reconstruct phased Snaketown expansion. Modern simulations of water delivery use assumptions and are not direct historical measurements. Research was undertaken with the Gila River Indian Community Cultural Resource Management Program and Pima-Maricopa Irrigation Project.

cases.actor_and_access_questions: Use Hohokam inhabitants as a source-supported collective when describing construction and cultivation; the paper explicitly says coordination and allocation arrangements are not established. Do not transfer the funding for the modern research project to ancient builders. Seek source-based O’odham and Piipaash community perspectives and original archaeological chronology; distinguish later settlement descendants and present-day institutions from the specific ancient construction event.

nearest_records.relationship: Another regional water-management case; a comparison, not evidence that the social institutions match.
Balinese spring-connected irrigation, not a Gila river diversion network.
Another American agricultural water landscape but distinct wetland field form; no transmission inferred.

cases.admission_assessment: Strong distinct North American regional canal/distribution case, subject to checking Woodson’s primary chronology and community attribution before asserting detailed dates or institutions.

not_selected: Dujiangyan and Sri Lankan tank cascades remain important open leads; they were not researched in depth in this preparatory pass.
